steps.text:
Here's the plan, pending your OK on the sizes:

1. Confirm the sizes on a dimension sheet (you gave the base, tip, rise and wall; the bend is my guess).
2. Build the spout as one sweep along the curved path, tapering from 22 mm to 9 mm with a 1.6 mm wall and both ends open.
3. Check the built part against the sheet.
4. Pick the printer and spool, slice, and queue only if you ask (queueing needs your OK).

steps.text: The sizes are confirmed. The tube needs two features: an outer tapered sweep, then an inner bore cut so the 1.6 mm wall stays even along the taper. I'll plan those before building.

assumptions: Base sits flat on the bed at z=0, straight 18 mm then a 60 degree arc of 60 mm centerline radius, tip ending 30 degrees above horizontal
Outer diameter tapers linearly from 22 mm to 9 mm along the path
Bore follows the outer taper so the wall stays 1.6 mm, tip bore 5.8 mm
Both ends open; bore extended past each end so no skin remains

steps.text:
I stopped the build because the part failed its wall check after the one allowed fix round.

**What's off:** The minimum wall check wants at least 0.8 mm (twice the 0.4 mm nozzle) and the part has 0.07 mm. The outer tube matches the sheet: 22 mm at the base, tapering to 9 mm at the tip over 70 mm of rise, and the body is closed. The thin spot is in the bore cut. My best guess is that the smooth spline I used for the bore's path bows slightly off the outer curve somewhere along the bend, so the wall pinches to almost nothing. The bore's measured diameter (18.35 mm) also doesn't match the 18.8 mm I set, which points the same way. I have not located the exact spot.

**Current state:** The design "Watering can spout" is open in SlicerX with the outer tube and the bore cut as two steps. It is not sliced or sent to a printer.

How do you want to go on? I can:
1. Rebuild the bore along an exact arc path (instead of a smooth spline) and check again.
2. Relax the bend, for example a larger bend radius, which keeps the wall more even and is more likely to pass.
3. Keep the design as is, and accept the thin spot to print with a finer check after slicing.
